records.name: Metrics
records.definition: Quantitative measurements a system emits about its state and behavior for monitoring and analysis.

records.name: Contracts

distinctFrom.reason: Contracts state the inputs, outputs and guarantees between components, while component boundaries are the edges those contracts sit on.
Contracts are agreements between particular components, while standards are conventions that many components conform to.

records.definition: Explicit, enforceable agreements specifying the inputs, outputs, and guarantees between components.

records.name: Independent Deployment

distinctFrom.reason: Independent deployment is releasing without coordinating others, while bounded context ownership is one team controlling one part of the system.
Independent deployment is releasing a component alone, while independent testing is exercising it alone.

records.definition: The ability to release a component to production without coordinating the deployment of others.

records.name: Delivery Speed
records.definition: The rate at which changes are delivered to production.

records.name: Boilerplate

distinctFrom.reason: Boilerplate is scaffolding written again in every use, while initial complexity is the structure of ports and adapters paid once before the first feature.

records.definition: Repetitive, mandatory scaffolding code that adds ceremony without domain value.

records.name: Schema

distinctFrom.reason: A schema is the formal definition of data, while the schemas tag names the file concern that holds such definitions.
A schema defines the structure data must take, while type metadata describes the field types a structure has at runtime.

records.definition: A formal definition of the structure, types, and constraints of data.

records.name: Compatibility
records.definition: The degree to which a component interoperates with other versions or systems without modification.

records.name: Cost
records.definition: The resource or financial expenditure required to build, run, or change a system.

records.name: Metadata
records.definition: Descriptive data about a system's structure, capabilities, or content, consumed to drive behavior.

records.name: Discovery

distinctFrom.reason: Discovery locates which components are available, while diagnostics inspects a running system's structure and state to find what is wrong.

records.definition: The ability to locate available components, services, or capabilities at runtime.

records.name: Iteration Speed
records.definition: The rate at which cycles of change and feedback can be completed.

records.name: Race Conditions

distinctFrom.reason: A race condition is any outcome that depends on interleaving, while a lost update is the particular case of one writer overwriting another.

records.definition: A defect where the outcome depends on the uncontrolled interleaving of concurrent operations.

records.name: Operational Complexity
records.definition: The effort and intricacy required to deploy, run, and maintain a system in production.

records.name: Standards

distinctFrom.reason: Standards are conventions components conform to, while a policy is rules on which actions are permitted or denied.

records.definition: Agreed conventions and specifications that components conform to for interoperability and consistency.

records.name: Single Point of Failure
records.definition: A component whose failure alone halts the entire system because it has no redundancy.

records.name: Debugging
records.definition: The activity of locating and diagnosing the cause of a defect.

records.name: Specification
records.definition: A precise, authoritative description of required behavior, structure, or interface.

records.name: False Positives
records.definition: Incorrect positive results reported when the detected condition is not present.

records.name: Ownership

distinctFrom.reason: Ownership assigns responsibility for a component to a team, while a canonical definition gives a fact one authoritative definition.

records.definition: A clear assignment of responsibility for a component to a person or team.

records.name: Silent Failure

distinctFrom.reason: A silent failure leaves no signal at all, while log-as-control-flow leaves a log line and carries on as if it were handled.
A silent failure emits nothing, while observability noise emits too much to act on.
A silent failure is any unsurfaced failure, while silent data corruption is invalid data accepted and stored unchecked.

records.definition: A failure that occurs without surfacing any error, log, or signal, leaving it undetected.

records.name: Message Contract
records.definition: The agreed schema and semantics of messages exchanged between components.

records.name: Replay

distinctFrom.reason: Replay reprocesses recorded events to rebuild state, while a temporal query asks what the state was at a given point.

records.definition: The ability to re-process a recorded sequence of events to reconstruct or recover state, including the state at a past point.

records.name: DSLs
records.definition: Domain-specific languages, small notations tailored to express solutions within one problem domain.

records.name: Acceptance Criteria
records.definition: Predefined conditions a deliverable must satisfy to be accepted as complete and correct.

records.name: Ambiguous Naming

distinctFrom.reason: Ambiguous naming is one identifier open to several readings, while an inconsistent error model is one failure reported in several shapes.

records.definition: Identifiers whose meaning is unclear or open to multiple interpretations, obscuring intent.

records.name: Automated Enforcement

distinctFrom.reason: Automated enforcement is any machine check that rules hold, while policy as code is writing the policies as the rules such a check evaluates.

records.definition: Machine-applied checking that rules and policies hold, catching violations without manual review.

records.name: Automation
records.definition: The execution of tasks by software or machinery without manual intervention.

records.name: Boolean Flag Soup
records.definition: Representing state through many interdependent boolean flags, producing tangled and invalid combinations.

records.name: Capacity Planning
records.definition: Forecasting resource demand and provisioning capacity to meet it without waste or shortfall.

records.name: Code Generation
records.definition: Producing source code automatically from a higher-level model, schema, or specification.

records.name: Composition Root
records.definition: The single startup location where an application's object graph is assembled and its dependencies wired.

records.name: Context

distinctFrom.reason: Context is the surrounding information that makes a record interpretable, while a decision record is one record that carries it.
Context is what surrounded a decision, while consequences are what follow from it.
Context is the circumstances a choice was made in, while the decision is the choice.
Context is the information attached to an entry, while structured events are entries written as machine-parsable records.

records.definition: The surrounding information and circumstances captured to make a decision, event, or log entry interpretable.

records.name: Continuous Processing
records.definition: Handling data incrementally as it arrives, rather than in discrete scheduled batches.

records.name: Controlled Access
records.definition: Mediated, restricted access to a resource so that only permitted operations reach it.

records.name: Controlled Evolution
records.definition: The managed, deliberate change of a system over time without breaking existing consumers.

records.name: Cross-Cutting Concerns
records.definition: Concerns such as logging, security, or transactions whose implementation spans many modules rather than localizing to one.

records.name: Damage Limitation
records.definition: Containing the blast radius of a failure or breach so its impact stays bounded.

records.name: Evaluation
records.definition: The systematic assessment of a model or system's behavior and quality against defined criteria.

records.name: Evidence
records.definition: Recorded proof that substantiates a claim, decision, or compliance requirement.

records.name: Explicit Inputs

distinctFrom.reason: Explicit inputs forbid reading ambient state during a call, while no hidden state forbids keeping state between calls.
Explicit inputs govern what a computation reads, while no side effects governs what it writes.

records.definition: All data a computation needs supplied through its parameters rather than read from ambient or hidden state.

records.name: Fallback
records.definition: An alternative path or default invoked automatically when the primary operation fails or is unavailable.

records.name: Independent Work Units
records.definition: Work partitioned into discrete units that execute in isolation, without shared mutable state or ordering dependencies.

records.name: Large Input Handling
records.definition: The ability to process inputs too large to fit in memory, through streaming or chunking.

records.name: Legal-Transition Enforcement
records.definition: Rejecting any state change that is not a permitted transition.

records.name: Plugins
records.definition: Independently-developed components that attach to a host at defined extension points to add capabilities.

records.name: Policy
records.definition: A declared set of rules governing what actions are permitted or denied within a system.

records.name: Recovery
records.definition: Restoring a system to correct operation or a consistent state after a failure.

records.name: Reuse
records.definition: Using an existing component, module, or solution in a new context rather than rebuilding it.

records.name: Runtime Indirection
records.definition: Resolving a binding or call target at runtime through an intermediary layer rather than a direct, static reference.

records.name: Safe Defaults

distinctFrom.reason: Safe defaults are the state shipped when nothing is changed, while fail safe is the state left behind when an operation fails.

records.definition: Choosing default configurations and behaviors that are safe when left unchanged.

records.name: Safe Refactoring
records.definition: Changing a system's internal structure with confidence that its observable behavior is preserved.

records.name: Safe Substitution
records.definition: Replacing a component or expression with an equivalent one without altering program correctness.

records.name: Model Drift
records.definition: The gradual loss of a model's fidelity to the reality it represents, as data or conditions change over time.

records.name: Stable Contracts
records.definition: Interfaces and agreements that remain unchanged over time so that consumers can depend on them safely.

records.name: Thresholds
records.definition: Configured boundary values that trigger an alert or action when a measured metric crosses them.

records.name: Time Budget
records.definition: A bounded maximum amount of time allotted for an operation to complete.

records.name: Time Cost
records.definition: The amount of time an activity requires, weighed as a cost against its benefit.

records.name: Type Metadata
records.definition: Descriptive data about the types of a structure's fields, available for inspection at runtime.

records.name: Undo/Redo

distinctFrom.reason: Undo and redo reverse and reapply an operation, while deferred execution runs a captured request later.
Undo reverses one operation, while snapshot and restore returns an object to a whole captured state.

records.definition: The ability to reverse a previously applied operation and to reapply it.

records.name: Name the Concept
records.definition: A technique for giving a recurring group of values or steps a name in the domain language and one home in the code.

records.name: Name Constant
records.definition: A technique for replacing an unexplained literal with a named constant that states its meaning.

records.name: Replace Boolean with Enum
records.definition: A technique for replacing a boolean parameter or flag with a closed set of named values.
